# The Architecture of Ordinary Moments

I've been thinking about the word "ordinary" lately, and how it's become almost an insult in our culture. We're constantly told to be extraordinary, to stand out, to make our mark on the world in some indelible way. But I wonder if we've gotten this entirely backward.

This morning, I watched my neighbor water his plants. Not metaphorical plants in some inspirational sense—actual plants on his actual porch. He spent twenty minutes doing it, adjusting the angle of his watering can, checking the soil with his fingers, moving one pot slightly to catch better light. He wasn't filming it. No one was watching. He was just... doing it. Perfectly, carefully, with the kind of attention usually reserved for things we consider important.

That's when it hit me: that *was* important. Not because it would lead anywhere or become something else, but because it was itself, completely and fully.

We've been sold this narrative that our lives are ladders. Every moment is either getting us closer to the top or wasting our time. But what if life isn't a ladder? What if it's more like a tapestry, and the ordinary moments are actually the threads that hold everything together?

I think about my father, who died five years ago. I can barely remember the big moments anymore—we went to Disney World once when I was eight, and I can recall maybe three disconnected images. But I remember him standing in the kitchen on a random Tuesday, making scrambled eggs while humming off-key. I remember the particular way he'd adjust his glasses before reading the newspaper. I remember his hands.

These memories are clearer than the supposedly "important" moments. They're clearer because they happened over and over. They're clearer because they were real in a way that planned experiences sometimes aren't.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *wabi-sabi* that celebrates impermanence and imperfection. It's finding beauty not in grand structures or perfect things, but in the temporary, the worn, the incomplete. A coffee cup with a slight chip. Morning light on a worn wooden table. A song played on an old guitar with slightly out-of-tune strings.

I think we need more of this. Not as an aesthetic movement, but as a way of being.

There's so much pressure to monetize our passions, to turn everything into content, to make our existence count in quantifiable ways. We're all supposed to be building personal brands, as though we're corporations. But maybe the real luxury in modern life is doing something with absolutely no audience, no metrics, no payoff except the doing of it.

I know someone who bakes bread every Saturday. Just for herself and her partner. She's not selling it, not posting pictures, not building a sourdough empire. She just loves the process—the smell, the feel of the dough, the rhythm of it. She has no interest in making it her "thing." And I think that's radical.

The word "radical" comes from "radix," meaning root. What could be more radical than returning to the roots of why we do anything—simply because we enjoy it, because it matters to us, because the doing is its own purpose?

I've noticed that the older people I know—those who seem to have some kind of peace—they're not the ones who achieved the most. They're the ones who found satisfaction in small things. My grandmother will spend an entire afternoon tending her garden, not because she needs the vegetables, but because she loves the work. My friend's father reads the same books over and over, deeply, rather than racing through new ones. These people aren't lazy or unambitious in destructive ways. They've just made peace with the fact that not everything needs to mean something beyond itself.

This isn't an argument against ambition or growth or trying to make the world better. But it's an argument against the tyranny of significance. Against the anxiety that every moment must either be productive or at least entertaining. Against the sense that if you're not constantly becoming someone new or achieving something visible, you're failing.

What if we're already enough? What if the moment you're in right now—reading these words, sitting wherever you are, breathing air—what if that's already the thing? Not preparation for the thing, not a stepping stone toward the thing, but the actual thing itself?

I think about the Buddha sitting under the Bodhi tree. For years, he wasn't going anywhere. He was just sitting. And somehow, in that radical ordinariness, everything became clear.

We could all sit under a tree, of course. We probably won't. And that's fine. But we could approach our actual lives—the ones we're already living—with that same quality of attention. We could water our plants like they matter. Cook dinner like someone will love us for it. Have a conversation like the other person's words are worth remembering.

These aren't small things, though they appear small. They're the only things, actually.

The poet William Carlos Williams wrote that "so much depends upon a red wheel barrow glazed with rain water beside the white chickens." He wasn't being ironic. He meant it. In that moment, paying attention to a wheelbarrow, he found everything that mattered.

So here's my thought, as the words pile up and I near my limit: be ordinary. Be radically, courageously ordinary. Find something you love that no one else needs to know about. Do it with attention. Notice the small things. Understand that your life is not a means to an end but an end in itself.

The world probably doesn't need another person desperate to matter. But it could use more people who are simply present, who do their small tasks with care, who understand that a life well-lived isn't measured in impact but in attention.

That's enough.
